title: A Prophet's Marriage and Three Names
overview: The LORD has the prophet Hosea marry and name his children as living messages about Israel's unfaithfulness, its coming fall, and a surprising promise of restoration.

parts.label: Who and when (v. 1)
parts.note: Hosea spoke mainly to Israel, the northern of the two Hebrew kingdoms, while it was rich and secure under King Jeroboam II in the 700s BC. The list of Judah's kings suggests his work spanned decades, as Israel slid toward its fall to Assyria in 722 BC.

parts.label: A marriage as a message (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: The LORD tells Hosea to marry Gomer, described with a Hebrew phrase about sexual unfaithfulness, so his home pictures Israel leaving its God for other gods. Translations differ on whether she was already unfaithful or became so later, and readers differ on whether this was a real marriage or a vision or parable.

parts.label: First son: Jezreel (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Jezreel was the royal town where, nearly a century earlier, Jehu slaughtered King Ahab's family to seize the throne, and the reigning king, Jeroboam II, was Jehu's great-grandson. An earlier book praises that coup (2 Kings 10:30), yet here the LORD holds Jehu's family to account for the bloodshed and warns that Israel's military might, its bow, will be broken.

parts.label: A daughter: Lo-Ruhamah (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Her name means "no compassion" or "not loved," a sign that the LORD's patience with Israel is running out. By contrast, Judah in the south will be saved by the LORD and not by weapons, which many readers link to Jerusalem surviving an Assyrian siege in 701 BC.

parts.label: Second son: Lo-Ammi (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: His name means "not my people," undoing the core promise of the covenant, the binding agreement that Israel would be the LORD's people and the LORD their God. The Hebrew of the last line can be read as "I will not be 'I am' for you," echoing God's name in Exodus 3:14, which is one reason translations word it differently.

parts.label: The names reversed (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: Then everything flips: Israel will be as countless as sand, those called "not my people" will be called children of the living God, the two kingdoms will reunite under one leader, and Jezreel, which means "God sows," now promises new growth. Jewish readers see a promised return and reunion of the people, while Christians, following Romans 9:25-26 and 1 Peter 2:10, also read it as God welcoming outsiders, including non-Jews, through Jesus.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promise of verses 10 and 11 is fulfilled in the church of Jews and non-Jews together, or still awaits a future restoration of the Jewish people as well.
think: When trust has been badly broken, what do you think it would take to turn "you are not mine" back into "you are mine"?
